{{Short description|Special point on a modular curve in mathematics}}
{{Expand German|Heegner-Punkt|fa=yes}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Heegner point''' is a point on a [[modular curve]] that is the image of a quadratic imaginary point of the [[upper half-plane]]. Heegner points were defined by [[Bryan Birch]] and named after [[Kurt Heegner]], who used similar ideas to prove [[Class number problem|Gauss's conjecture]] on imaginary [[quadratic fields]] of class number one.

==Gross–Zagier theorem==
The '''Gross–Zagier theorem''' {{harv|Gross|Zagier|1986}} describes the [[Néron–Tate height|height]] of  Heegner points in terms of a derivative of the [[L-function]] of the elliptic curve at the point ''s''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1. In particular if the elliptic curve has (analytic) rank 1, then the Heegner points can be used to construct a rational point on the curve of infinite order (so the [[Mordell–Weil group]] has rank at least 1). More generally, {{harvtxt|Gross|Kohnen|Zagier|1987}} showed that Heegner points could be used to construct [[rational point]]s on the curve for each positive integer ''n'', and the heights of these points were the coefficients of a modular form of weight&nbsp;3/2. [[Shou-Wu Zhang]] generalized the Gross–Zagier theorem from elliptic curves to the case of modular [[abelian variety|abelian varieties]] ({{harvs|nb|last=Zhang |year1=2001 |year2=2004}}, {{harvs|nb|last1=Yuan|authorlink1=Xinyi Yuan|last2=Zhang|last3=Zhang|authorlink3=Wei Zhang (mathematician)|year=2009}}).

==Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture==
[[Kolyvagin]] later used Heegner points to construct [[Euler system]]s, and used this to prove much of the [[Birch&ndash;Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture]] for rank 1 elliptic curves. Brown proved the [[Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture]] for most rank 1 elliptic curves over global fields of positive characteristic {{harv|Brown|1994}}.

==Computation==
Heegner points can be used to compute very large rational points on rank 1 elliptic curves (see {{harv|Watkins|2006}} for a survey) that could not be found by naive methods. Implementations of the algorithm are available in [[Magma computer algebra system|Magma]], [[PARI/GP]], and [[Sage (computer algebra system)|Sage]].
